message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.008 u (average; protium ≈ 1.0079 u) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Isotopes** | Protium (¹H, 99.98 %), Deuterium (²H, 0.02 %) and Tritium (³H, radioactive) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈ 0.00008988 g cm⁻³) |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 24.587 eV (2375 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative → energy released when gaining an electron) |
| **Heat capacity (Cp)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low as a gas; becomes metallic under extreme pressure (~400 GPa) |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids, and many nonmetals; reacts with oxygen to form water (combustion). |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; burns with a pale blue flame; can form explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air). |
| **Bonding** | Exists as a diatomic molecule (H₂) under normal conditions; forms covalent bonds in organic compounds (C–H, N–H, O–H). |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) – key in astrophysics. |
| **Applications** | Fuel cell technology, rocket propellant, hydrogenation reactions, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents), semiconductor manufacturing, etc. |

**Key Takeaways**

- Hydrogen is the lightest element, existing naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂) at room temperature.
- It has a very low density, high ionization energy, and is highly reactive, especially with oxygen.
- Its isotopes (deuterium, tritium) are used in nuclear fusion research and as tracers in chemistry and biology.
- Hydrogen’s spectral lines are fundamental to astronomy and plasma physics.
